For an integer \(t\ge 2\), consider all integers \(k\ge t\), finite sets \(V\), and families \(\mathcal F\) of \(k\)-element subsets of \(V\) with the following properties. The family is intersecting, meaning that \(F\cap F'\ne\varnothing\) for all \(F,F'\in\mathcal F\). Its covering number is \(t\), where the covering number is the minimum cardinality of a set \(C\subseteq V\) meeting every member of \(\mathcal F\).

In addition, choose a partition \(\mathcal F=\mathcal F_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\mathcal F_t\) into nonempty subfamilies and pairwise disjoint nonempty sets \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\subseteq V\) such that \(X_i\subseteq F\) for every \(F\in\mathcal F_i\). Define
\[
b(t)=\min\sum_{i=1}^{t}\bigl(k-|X_i|\bigr),
\]
where the minimum ranges over all the choices just described, including \(k\) and \(V\).

With \(\log\) denoting the natural logarithm, determine the exact value of
\[
\lim_{\substack{t\to\infty\\t\in\mathbb Z}}\frac{\log b(t)}{\log t}.
\]
</problem>

24	## 1. Lower bound

38	### Counting small deficits

46	Suppose instead that \(s>d(d+2)\) groups have deficit at most \(d\), and let \(\mathcal G\) be their union. By (1), \(\tau(\mathcal G)=s\).

Consequently, \(F\) has at least \(d+1\) points outside its own core, contradicting its deficit being at most \(d\). This proves (2).

81	## 2. A random block lemma
82	
83	Fix \(n\ge100\), and set
84	\[
85	r=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil,\qquad L=\lceil\log n\rceil,\qquad m=100nL.
86	\]
87	
88	We need an indexed sequence \(B_1,\ldots,B_m\) of \(r\)-subsets of \([n]\), satisfying:
89	
90	1. Every pair of distinct vertices occurs together in at least \(10L\) blocks.
91	2. Every vertex occurs in at most \(200rL\) blocks.
92	3. For every \(A\subseteq[m]\) and \(J\subseteq[n]\) with \(|A|=|J|=r\),
93	   \[
94	   \sum_{a\in A}|B_a\cap J|<5Lr.
95	   \tag{4}
96	   \]
97	
98	Repeated blocks are allowed; their indices remain distinct.
99	
100	### Proof of existence
101	
102	Choose the \(B_a\) independently and uniformly among the \(r\)-subsets of \([n]\). We use
103	\[
104	\frac{r(r-1)}{n-1}\ge\frac12,\qquad r^2\le2n.
105	\tag{5}
106	\]
107	
108	For a binomial random variable \(X\) of mean \(\mu\),
109	\[
110	\mathbb E e^{sX}\le \exp\bigl(\mu(e^s-1)\bigr),
111	\tag{6}
112	\]
113	which follows from \(1+u\le e^u\).
114	
115	For a fixed pair of vertices, its codegree has mean
116	\[
117	\mu=100L\frac{r(r-1)}{n-1}\ge50L.
118	\]
119	By Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{-X}\), using \(e>5/2\),
120	\[
121	\Pr(X<10L)
122	\le e^{10L-\mu(1-e^{-1})}
123	\le e^{-20L}.
124	\tag{7}
125	\]
126	
127	A fixed vertex has degree of mean \(100rL\). Applying (6) with \(s=1\), and using \(e<11/4\),
128	\[
129	\Pr(X>200rL)
130	\le \exp\bigl(100rL(e-3)\bigr)
131	\le e^{-25rL}.
132	\tag{8}
133	\]
134	
135	Now fix \(A,J\) of size \(r\), and let
136	\[
137	T=\sum_{a\in A}|B_a\cap J|,\qquad h=5Lr.
138	\]
139	If \(T\ge h\), some \(h\) of the \(r^2\) possible block–vertex incidences occur. Any specified \(h\) incidences have probability at most \((r/n)^h\): within a block,
140	\[
141	\frac{(r)_a}{(n)_a}\le (r/n)^a,
142	\]
143	and different blocks are independent. Thus, if \(h\le r^2\),
144	\[
145	\Pr(T\ge h)
146	\le \binom{r^2}{h}(r/n)^h
147	\le \left(\frac{er^3}{nh}\right)^h
148	\le \left(\frac{2e}{5L}\right)^{5Lr}
149	\le e^{-5Lr}.
150	\tag{9}
151	\]
152	If \(h>r^2\), the event is impossible, so the same bound holds.
153	
154	There are at most \((mn)^r\) choices of \(A,J\). Since \(L\ge5\),
155	\[
156	\log(mn)=\log100+2\log n+\log L\le4L.
157	\]
158	The probability that (4) fails is therefore at most \(e^{-Lr}\).
159	
160	Combining all three failure probabilities, we obtain
161	\[
162	\Pr(\text{some property fails})
163	\le n^2e^{-20L}+ne^{-25rL}+e^{-Lr}
164	\le n^{-18}+n^{-249}+n^{-10}<1.
165	\]
166	Hence a block sequence with all three properties exists. ∎

168	## 3. Turning the blocks into the required family
169	
170	Fix such a block sequence. Write
171	\[
172	P_i=\{a:i\in B_a\},\qquad c_{ij}=|P_i\cap P_j|.
173	\]
174	Thus
175	\[
176	|P_i|\le200rL,\qquad c_{ij}\ge10L.
177	\]
178	
179	For \(T\subseteq P_i\), \(|T|\le r\), define
180	\[
181	J_i(T)=
182	\left\{j\ne i:
183	2|T\cap P_j|\ge c_{ij}\right\}.
184	\tag{10}
185	\]
186	Property (4) implies
187	\[
188	|J_i(T)|<r.
189	\tag{11}
190	\]
191	Indeed, otherwise choose \(r\) vertices from \(J_i(T)\). Their total incidence with the blocks indexed by \(T\) is at least \(5Lr\); extend \(T\) to \(r\) block indices and contradict (4).
192	
193	Set
194	\[
195	d=r(200L+1).
196	\]
197	
198	Take pairwise disjoint cores \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), each of size \(n\). Also take:
199	
200	- a distinct point \(z_a\) for every block index \(a\);
201	- private reservoirs \(Y_i\), each of size \(n+d\).
202	
203	All these sets and points are mutually disjoint.
204	
205	A **base edge of group \(i\)** is obtained as follows:
206	
207	- choose \(T\subseteq P_i\), \(|T|\le r\);
208	- include all of \(X_i\);
209	- include \(z_a\) for every \(a\in P_i\setminus T\);
210	- for each \(j\in J_i(T)\), include one arbitrarily chosen point of \(X_j\).
211	
212	Its number of points outside \(X_i\) is
213	\[
214	s=|P_i|-|T|+|J_i(T)|<d.
215	\]

217	\[
218	k=n+d
219	\]
220	by adding any \(d-s\) points from \(Y_i\). Include **all** such choices in \(\mathcal F_i\).
221	
222	These are finite, nonempty, \(k\)-uniform families. An edge of group \(i\) contains at most one point of every other core, so it cannot belong to another group.
223	
224	### Intersecting property
225	
226	Two edges of the same group share their core.
227	
228	Consider edges of different groups \(i,j\), with choices \(T_i,T_j\). If some
229	\[
230	a\in P_i\cap P_j
231	\]
232	belongs to neither \(T_i\) nor \(T_j\), both edges contain \(z_a\).
233	
234	Otherwise \(T_i\cup T_j\) contains all \(c_{ij}\) common block indices. Thus at least one of
235	\[
236	|T_i\cap P_j|,\qquad |T_j\cap P_i|
237	\]
238	is at least \(c_{ij}/2\). By (10), one edge contains a point of the other's core. They again intersect.
239	
240	### Covering number
241	
242	Choosing one point from each core gives a cover of size \(n\).
243	
244	Conversely, let \(C\) have size at most \(n-1\). Put
245	\[
246	U=\{i:C\cap X_i=\varnothing\},\qquad
247	Z=\{a:z_a\in C\}.
248	\]
249	Since each hit core consumes a different point of \(C\),
250	\[
251	|U|>|Z|.
252	\]
253	Moreover,
254	\[
255	\sum_{i\in U}|Z\cap P_i|
256	=\sum_{a\in Z}|B_a\cap U|
257	\le r|Z|<r|U|.
258	\]
259	Hence some \(i\in U\) satisfies
260	\[
261	|Z\cap P_i|<r.
262	\]
263	Choose \(T=Z\cap P_i\). Then every included \(z_a\) avoids \(C\).
264	
265	For every required core contact, choose its point outside \(C\); this is possible because each core has \(n>|C|\) points. Finally choose the padding outside \(C\), possible because
266	\[
267	|Y_i\setminus C|\ge d+1.
268	\]
269	The resulting edge avoids \(C\). Therefore
270	\[
271	\tau(\mathcal F)=n.
272	\]
273	
274	Every group has deficit \(d\), so
275	\[
276	b(n)\le nd
277	=n\lceil\sqrt n\rceil(200\lceil\log n\rceil+1).
278	\tag{12}
279	\]
280	
281	Equations (3) and (12) prove the claimed limit.
282	
283	## 4. Executable checks
284	
285	The following self-contained Python audits:

288	- the numerical inequalities used in the probability estimates;
